proof:
# Optimized triple reflection excludes below-half extraction through six fibers

For an actual convex body with n=d=1, positive mixed length M=H_1(S)>0,
and at most SIX positive integer interval fibers (1<=N<=6), the maximum mass of a convex subbody with true integer
centroid and local half-depth is at least half the original mixed mass.
For exactly five positive fibers a stronger 4/7 retained fraction holds.
No assertion for an arbitrary number of positive fibers is made.

The new local ingredient optimizes the continuous reflection center of
a compatible triple. It is stronger than the archived bound which fixes
the middle-fiber midpoint. The aggregation below is classical finite
concavity arithmetic, not numerical evidence.

Let I_i be the positive interval fibers of C, indexed consecutively by
0,...,N-1, and let w_i=|I_i|>0, M=sum w_i. The sequence w is concave.
For a mixed point (j,y), set

    R(j,y)=sum_i |I_i intersect (2y-I_(2j-i))|,
    R_*=max_(j,y) R(j,y).

Missing and zero-length fibers contribute zero. The exact reflection
intersection is convex and symmetric, so R_* is attainable by a locally
half-deep extraction, using exact one-sided thickening if necessary.
Conversely the proved interval half-depth rigidity bounds every locally
half-deep extraction by reflection retention at its centroid. Thus R_*
is exactly the maximum local-gamma_1 extraction mass. These facts are
proved in `candidate f9fd3b8e5ea799fa`.

## 1. A sharp optimized-middle triple bound

Take three symmetric base indices j-k,j,j+k, with endpoint lengths a,c
and middle length b. Compatibility gives (I_(j-k)+I_(j+k))/2 subset I_j,
so b>=(a+c)/2. Put

    l=min(a,c), A=max(a,c).

The contribution of these three fibers alone admits a center y in I_j
with retained mass at least

    F(a,b,c)=max{b, 2l+min(b,A)}.                   (1)

Consequently R_*>=F(a,b,c), even when other fibers are present.

Translate the continuous coordinate to make I_j=[0,b]. The midpoint
interval of the endpoint pair is J=[s,s+(a+c)/2], with
0<=s<=b-(a+c)/2. The endpoint overlap is maximal, of length l, exactly
when the reflection center belongs to the plateau

    P=[s+l/2,s+A/2].

The two ordered endpoint contributions then sum to 2l. The self-overlap
of [0,b] at y is 2 min(y,b-y). Put q=min(b,A); its level set at least q
is the closed interval

    Q=[q/2,b-q/2].

These intervals ALWAYS intersect: the right endpoint of P is at least
A/2>=q/2, and its left endpoint is at most
b-(a+c)/2+l/2=b-A/2<=b-q/2. At a point of P intersect Q the retained
mass is at least 2l+q. The own-fiber midpoint separately retains b.
This proves (1) with actual closed interval overlaps, including all
plateau endpoints.

The bound is sharp for fixed lengths as a bound on the optimized
THREE-FIBER contribution at the middle base. Take the endpoint intervals
[0,a],[0,c] and middle interval [0,b]. The endpoint contribution is a
trapezoid supported on [0,(a+c)/2], of height2l and plateau[l/2,A/2].
If A>=b the own midpoint is on the plateau, giving maximum b+2l.
If A<=b the maximum on the plateau occurs at A/2 and is A+2l; on either
side the piecewise slopes show that the only competing maximum is b
at the own midpoint. Thus the optimized middle contribution is exactly
F(a,b,c). Larger own endpoint fibers can of course give a larger GLOBAL
reflection maximum.

## 2. Four positive fibers

Write the widths as (a,b,c,d). Reflect the base order if necessary to
arrange b>=c. Concavity then gives d<=c, since 2c>=b+d.

If a>=c, put L=max(a,b) and h=min(a,b). Formula (1) at the first middle
base gives R_*>=h+2c, while the largest own fiber gives R_*>=L. If
L>=M/2 there is nothing to prove. Otherwise L<h+c+d, hence

    M/2<h+c+d<=h+2c<=R_*.

If a<=c, the largest width is b. Formula (1) at the two middle bases
provides R_*>=c+2a and R_*>=c+2d. Unless b>=M/2, one has b<a+c+d and

    M/2<a+c+d<=c+2max(a,d)<=R_*.

Thus four fibers always give R_*>=M/2, and the inequality is strict if
EVERY original fiber has mass strictly below M/2. No fiber-position
assumption beyond actual convex compatibility was used.

The half constant can occur with all four fibers positive: for the
actual intervals [0,w_i] with widths (1,5,3,1), formula (1)'s sharp
placement calculation at both middle bases gives maximum5, the extreme
bases retain only1, and M=10. Each middle base has only one reflected
endpoint pair, so this is a complete exact calculation of R_*=5.

## 3. A common observation about the third-largest width

Let t be the third-largest width of a concave sequence with N>=3.
Its superlevel set {i:w_i>=t} is an interval of indices with at least
three members. There are therefore THREE CONSECUTIVE widths at least t.
Formula (1) applied to those three gives

    R_*>=3t.                                       (2)

Also the strict superlevel set {i:w_i>t} is consecutive and has at most
two members. It can be placed inside a block of two adjacent indices.
Both observations allow ties and need no genericity assumption.

## 4. Five positive fibers: R_*>=4M/7

Use indices0,...,4 and the third-largest t. If w_2<=t, concavity and
symmetry about index2 give

    M<=5w_2<=5t,

so (2) gives R_*>=3M/5>=4M/7.

Otherwise the indices of the two largest widths can, after reversing
order, be taken as1,2. Write

    (w_0,w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4)=(a,b,c,d,e),
    T=max(a,d).

Then b,c>=T and e<=d. Formula (1) at bases1 and2 gives

    R_*>=min(b,c)+2T.                              (3)

If b>=c, concavity gives b<=2c-d and e<=2d-c. Therefore

    M<=a+2c+2d<=2c+3T.

Nonnegativity of e and the second inequality also give c<=2d<=2T, so

    2c+3T<=(7/4)(c+2T)<=(7/4)R_*.

If c>=b, then c+e<=2d and b>=T, whence

    M<=a+b+3d<=b+4T<=(5/3)(b+2T)<=(5/3)R_*.

This proves the stated 4/7 bound in every case.

The constant4/7 is sharp as a limit of FIVE POSITIVE fibers. For
epsilon>0 take widths

    (1+epsilon,3+epsilon,2+epsilon,1+epsilon,epsilon)

and intervals [0,w_i]. The upper slopes are2,-1,-1,-1, so these are an
actual convex-compatible family. At bases1 and3 there is one reflected
pair, with maxima4+3epsilon and1+3epsilon. At base2 the inner triple
contributes at most4+3epsilon by the sharp placement in Section1; the
remaining outer pair adds at most2epsilon. Extreme bases retain at most
1+epsilon. Thus R_*<=4+5epsilon, while M=7+5epsilon. The lower bound just
proved and this upper bound show R_*/M tends to4/7. No claim about the
exact maximizing center for positive epsilon is needed.

## 5. Six positive fibers: R_*>=M/2

Use indices0,...,5 and the third-largest t. Put

    q_i=w_i-2w_(i+1)+w_(i+2)<=0,  i=0,1,2,3.

The following exact concavity quadratures will be used:

    M-3(w_2+w_3)=q_0+3q_1+3q_2+q_3<=0,
    M-(w_0+5w_3)=q_1+3q_2+q_3<=0,
    M-3(w_1+w_4)=q_0+q_3<=0.                       (4)

Place {i:w_i>t} inside an adjacent two-index block. By reversal there
are only three cases. If the block is{0,1}, then w_2,w_3<=t and the
first inequality gives M<=6t. If it is{1,2}, then w_0,w_3<=t and the
second gives M<=6t. If it is{2,3}, then w_1,w_4<=t and the third gives
M<=6t. The reversed cases follow by reflecting (4).

Together with (2), this yields R_*>=3t>=M/2. This six-fiber bound is
not claimed sharp for exactly six positive fibers; it is a proved
finite-support exclusion of a below-half maximum extraction.

## 6. Budget-sensitive conclusion and scope

One or two positive fibers are settled by a largest fiber, and the
three-fiber half bound was proved in
`candidate ad15334eed60c161`.
Sections2--5 therefore prove the half-mass extraction statement for
EVERY body with at most six positive interval fibers.

Equivalently, a hypothetical global local-gamma_1 maximum extraction
with mass strictly below M/2 must come from an original body with at
least SEVEN positive integer fibers. This uses the original total mass
in the finite inequalities; it does not assert that objective-one
contact equations or an unused interior point alone force improvement.

The construction is a reflection intersection at an actual integer base
and an actual continuous center. Its symmetry supplies the local
half-depth property without an OC hypothesis. Hence it also gives an
original-source OC center in this bounded n=d=1 class. The unrestricted
number-of-fibers problem and arbitrary n,d remain unproved here.
